title: Sonnet 33 in the sequence
short: This is the first of a group (33-36) in which the speaker responds to some fault or betrayal by the young man. It was printed in the 1609 Quarto.
body: Sonnets 33-35 deal with an offence the young man has committed against the speaker, which is never named. Sonnet 34 continues the weather image ('Why didst thou promise such a beauteous day'), and 35 begins 'No more be grieved at that which thou hast done'. Sonnet 33 is one extended simile: an octave about the sun, a quatrain applying it to 'my sun', and a forgiving couplet. 'Full many' is an intensive idiom meaning 'very many'. Some, including Michael Wood, have linked the poem to the death of Shakespeare's son Hamnet (1596) through a sun/son pun, but that reading is speculative.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: Flatter
short: The sun 'flatters' the peaks: it pleases and caresses them. The word also hints at a courtier's false praise.
body: 'Flatter' sets the courtly tone of the octave, in which the sun is a monarch handing out favour with its 'sovereign eye'. Commentators note that flattery implies something false or short-lived in that favour, which prepares for its withdrawal. Flattery was a constant worry of Tudor court writing, and the word warns from the start that the sun's kindness may not be what it seems. The verbs of the first quatrain, 'Flatter', 'Kissing', 'Gilding', all describe tender or glamorous actions, and the octave's list of graces makes their loss harder to bear.

title: The sun as monarch
short: The sun is a king whose glance gives favour. 'Sovereign' means royal and also supremely effective, as in 'a sovereign remedy'.
body: Comparing the sun to a king, and a king to the sun, was a commonplace of Tudor political imagery, and Shakespeare's history plays use it (compare Richard II 3.2). The sun's 'eye' is its face or disc. The image lets the young man's later neglect be read as the withdrawal of a patron's or a king's favour. 'Sovereign' also hints at healing.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Heavenly alchemy
short: Sunlight gilds the pale streams, just as alchemy was supposed to turn base metal into gold. The sun transforms whatever it looks on.
body: Alchemy tried to turn base metals into gold, and the alchemists' sign for gold was the sun (Sol). The sun's 'golden face' (l. 3) 'gilds' the streams. But the change is only on the surface, a gilding, which hints that the beloved's favour may also be a show. Compare Sonnet 114, where the speaker's eye practises a flattering 'alchemy'. The word thus carries both the sun's power and a doubt about it.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
John Kerrigan, ed., The Sonnets and A Lover's Complaint (Penguin, 1986), commentary

title: The basest clouds
short: The lowest, meanest clouds are 'permitted' to ride across the sun's face. Prince Hal uses the same figure for his own hidden glory.
body: 'Base' means low in position and also low in rank. In 1 Henry IV 1.2 Hal compares himself to the sun 'Who doth permit the base contagious clouds / To smother up his beauty from the world'. The parallel suggests that the sun allows itself to be covered, so the young man is answerable for the company he keeps. 'Anon' means soon after.

sources.cite: William Shakespeare, 1 Henry IV 1.2 (Hal's soliloquy)

title: rack
short: 'Rack' means a mass of cloud driven by the wind, here a dark, fast-moving bank of cloud across the sun's face.
body: Malone glossed 'rack' as the quick motion of the clouds, and the OED records the sense of drifting cloud. Compare Hamlet 2.2 ('the rack stand still') and The Tempest 4.1 ('Leave not a rack behind'). The sun's 'celestial face' is spoiled by an 'ugly' covering, which may suggest disgrace, scandal, or a blemish on the face. 'Ride' (l. 5) adds a picture of a mounted troop.

title: forlorn
short: 'Forlorn' means abandoned and desolate: the world is left without the sun's light.
body: The word comes from Old English forloren, 'utterly lost'. The world is 'forlorn' because the sun has hidden his face, and the line looks ahead to the abandoned speaker. The sun 'Stealing unseen to west' (l. 8) sets in secret, slipping away like a guilty person. 'Disgrace' means both disfigurement and dishonour. The sun 'hides' its face, as God hides his face from the sinner in the Psalms.

title: My sun
short: The simile turns. The beloved is the speaker's sun, who shone on him briefly and was then hidden.
body: The third quatrain applies the octave to the speaker's own experience. 'One early morn' suggests a short, early spell of favour, and 'triumphant splendour on my brow' pictures the beloved's glory crowning him. The sun/son pun is hidden here and comes into the open in the couplet. The movement from 'Full many' mornings in the octave to 'one early morn' narrows the scale from the whole world to the speaker's own life. The change of tense to the past also suggests that this brief morning is already over.

Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: out! alack!
short: These are cries of grief and reproach: 'out!' expresses indignation or lament, and 'alack' sorrow.
body: As an exclamation 'out' expresses dismay or anger (compare Lady Macbeth's 'Out, damned spot'). 'Alack' expresses regret. In 'he was but one hour mine', the favour is very brief; 'one hour' may simply be an exaggeration. The two exclamations break the smooth descriptive syntax of the octave: this is the only point where the speaker cries out instead of reasoning, and the outburst prepares for the strained forgiveness of the couplet. The irregular stresses of 'But out! alack!' also break the iambic rhythm.

title: region cloud
short: This is the cloud of the upper air. 'Region' was a technical term for one of the layers of the air or sky.
body: Older cosmology divided the air into lower, middle and upper 'regions', so a 'region cloud' is a cloud high in the sky. Compare Hamlet 2.2: 'the region kites' and 'the dreadful thunder / Doth rend the region'. The cloud 'hath mask'd him': 'mask' means to conceal and also to disguise, as in a court masque. The cloud is high and distant, beyond the speaker's reach.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'region, n.'

title: no whit
short: 'No whit' means 'not at all', since a whit is the smallest part. The speaker's love does not despise the beloved for his fault.
body: 'Whit' comes from Old English wiht, 'thing, creature', and survives in 'not a whit'. The couplet turns to forgiveness, but the logic is strained: the comparison that excuses the beloved also admits that he is stained. The verb 'disdaineth' and its rhyme word 'staineth' are feminine endings (unstressed final syllables), which soften the close. The archaic -eth forms give the couplet the tone of a formal maxim or proverb.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'whit, n.'
Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

anchor: Suns of the world may stain
title: Suns ... stain
short: If the sun in heaven can be stained, earthly 'suns' (and 'sons' of men) may be too. 'Stain' means grow dim and also be defiled.
body: 'Stain' is used without an object, both of the sun being darkened and of a moral blot. Most editors notice the pun on 'suns' and 'sons', the men of the world. Critics disagree about the couplet's tone. Some hear generous forgiveness. Booth and others stress that the excuse is also an accusation, since 'stain' admits a moral fault and the forgiveness leans on a cosmic precedent. Sonnet 34 shows that the hurt is not over.
